title: Region controller lag triggered route ripple and mitigations
creator: Ananya Patel
body:
Summary:
On 2026-02-08 at ~09:13 UTC we observed a rapid increase in cross-region routing churn that produced a sustained spike in fallback model variant traffic and elevated tail latency for customers in EU and APAC regions. The root cause was a transient processing backlog in the region controller that delayed decommission and weight-update propagation. Delayed controller acknowledgements caused many proxy agents to re-evaluate locality weights simultaneously, creating a wave of regional handoffs and a short period of variant fallbacks as capacity briefly appeared constrained.

Impact:
- Duration: ~42 minutes of elevated error-rate and higher fallback invocation (09:13–09:55 UTC).
- Affected: ~18% of production request volume globally, concentrated in EU-West and APAC regions.
- Symptom: increased token latency (p95 up 3x), higher per-request cost due to fallback to larger variants, and transient 502/503 responses on some routes.

Timeline (high level):
- 09:12 UTC: Health monitors for region-controller queue length cross threshold.
- 09:13 UTC: Automated paging triggered; initial alert noted slow control-plane heartbeats from eu-west-1 controller instance.
- 09:17 UTC: Proxy fleet began local rebalancing as controller heartbeats missed >2 cycles, causing many routes to migrate to alternate regions/tier variants.
- 09:25 UTC: Fallback surge detected (metric: fallback_rate_global) and token latency p95 climbed. On-call applied temporary global rollout hold and increased capacity in eu-west and apac pools.
- 09:33 UTC: Identified controller GC pause and a delayed compatibility mapping refresh as proximate causes for backlog.
- 09:46 UTC: Controller replicas restored; queues drained and route churn dampened.
- 09:55 UTC: Metrics back within normal bounds; incident declared mitigated.

Root cause analysis:
Primary cause: a long GC pause (Java GC due to evolving agent metadata size spikes during a background compatibility-mapping refresh) on a region-controller replica which caused event processing latency to exceed heartbeat timeouts. The controller's backlog of weight/decommission events then replayed in a compressed window once the replica recovered, producing synchronized weight changes across proxies.
Contributing factors:
- Compatibility mapping refresh triggered with no rate limiting; the refresh expanded internal metadata by ~4x for a short period (recent schema change in model-compatibility table).
- Controller lacked admission control for incoming weight/decommission streams, so transient bursts were processed at full speed on recovery.
- Proxies use a conservative local reconvergence algorithm that aggressively re-routed when heartbeats were missed (aggressive fallback on perceived locality loss).
- Insufficient observability around per-replica event queue depth and replay velocity.

Mitigation performed during incident:
- 09:25 UTC: Applied global rollout hold to freeze new routing decisions and prevent further churn.
- 09:27 UTC: Scaled eu-west and apac capacity pools by adding spare capacity nodes (manual allocation).
- 09:33 UTC: Rebooted the affected controller replica and applied temporary GC tuning via JVM flag override to reduce pause times.
- 09:38 UTC: Enabled conservative proxy reconvergence feature flag to limit simultaneous re-routing while controllers reconciled.

Permanent fixes and action items (owners assigned):
1) Rate-limit compatibility mapping refreshes and break large refreshes into chunked diffs (owner: backend-data, PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/compat-mapper/pull/214) — due 2026-03-05.
2) Add admission control and exponential backoff on controller event replay so recovered replicas spread their replay over time (owner: control-plane, PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/controller/pull/512) — due 2026-02-28.
3) Implement per-replica queue-length and replay-velocity metrics + alerts (owner: observability, dashboard: https://redwood.grafana.net/d/ctrl/replica-queue) — due 2026-02-20.
4) Proxy-side: implement softened reconvergence (randomized delay window) to avoid global synchronized reroutes (owner: runtime-proxy, PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/proxy/pull/998) — due 2026-03-12.
5) Introduce a temporary canary gate for compatibility-mapping schema changes to validate metadata growth in staging before prod rollout (owner: infra-sheriffs) — due 2026-03-01.
6) Long term: redesign compatibility mapping to use compact diffs and streaming reconciliation (owner: platform-architecture) — RFC planned by 2026-04-01.

Post-incident review notes:
- The incident was non-deterministic and amplified by multiple small issues aligning (metadata growth + unthrottled replay + aggressive proxy behavior).
- Our existing controller failover assumed replays would be low-velocity; that assumption needs to be codified and enforced.
- Observability gaps made root-cause identification slower than necessary; adding an SLO for controller-queue-drain-time may help.

Follow-ups completed by update date:
- Observability team added replica queue metrics and an initial alert rule (2026-02-12).
- Controller team merged admission-control patch behind feature flag (2026-02-16); rolled to prod with a staged rollout finished 2026-02-18.
- Proxy team merged softened reconvergence and enabled it globally 2026-02-19.

Action owners and verification plan:
- control-plane (Lena Rodriguez): verify backoffs under synthetic load and confirm no route ripple in canary ring. Verification steps: simulated controller pause via chaos job + watch reroute metric (due 2026-02-25).
- observability (Marcus Chen): confirm alerts fire on queue depth and create dashboard panels for replay velocity (done 2026-02-12).
- runtime-proxy (Eleni Marquez): run 48-hour canary in eu-west staging to assert reduced synchronized reroutes (due 2026-02-26).

Lessons learned:
- Avoid assumptions of low-velocity replays — always plan for graceful throttling when a control-plane replica recovers.
- Prefer incremental metadata updates vs full refreshes for large mapping tables.
- Softening local reconvergence behavior significantly reduces amplification risk.

Conclusion:
This incident reinforced that small operational variance (GC pauses, metadata growth) can produce outsized routing churn when multiple components lack smoothing or backpressure. The mitigations and follow-ups reduce the blast radius and add guardrails to prevent synchronized re-routes on controller recovery. We consider the primary mitigations implemented and verified; remaining work is scheduled per the action items above.
